A FEW DEFINITIONS… / Green logistics describes all attempts to measure and minimize the ecological / impact of logistics activities. This includes all activities of the forward and reverse / flows of products, information, and services between the point of origin and the / point of consumption. / “Sustainable logistics” refers to the practices and processes aimed at / improving the sustainability of supply-chain activities, ranging from the / supply of raw materials to the transformation processes, the storage, the / packaging, the distribution and the management of the end of the lifecycle / of products. / Sustainable logistics is essentially about making logistics, freight, and / transportation more sustainable by minimizing the environmental impact of the / practices involved in these processes. / Sustainable Logistics (Fall) 2026 - Introduction 29

SUSTAINABLE OPERATIONS AND SUPPLY CHAINS / What is Sustainable Logistics… / Sustainable logistics, also known as green logistics or eco-friendly logistics, refers to the / practice of conducting logistical activities in an environmentally and socially responsible / manner. The goal is to minimize the negative impact of logistics operations on the environment, / society, and economy while optimizing the efficiency of the supply chain. Sustainable logistics / aims to reduce carbon emissions, resource consumption, and waste generation throughout the / entire supply chain process. / The potential benefits… / By adopting sustainable logistics practices, businesses can not only reduce their / environmental footprint but also improve their overall efficiency, reduce costs, and / enhance their brand image by aligning with the growing consumer demand for / environmentally responsible products and services. / Sustainable Logistics (Fall) 2026 - Introduction 32

Tecvia Media / Decarbonisation in Fleet Operations / Database / However, the data situation is less clear-cut than it may appear at first glance: No current, / Europe-wide harmonised stock statistics are published specifically for commercial vehicles over / 18 tonnes, broken down by Diesel, CNG, LNG, battery-electric, fuel cell and hydrogen / combustion engines. / The most reliable figures relate either to all trucks over 3.5 tonnes or to EU vehicle classes N2 / and N3. CNG and LNG are often grouped together as “Natural Gas” in vehicle stock data, while / hydrogen is usually reported without distinguishing between fuel-cell and internal-combustion / powertrains. / Most reliable overall overview: EU truck fleet 2023 / According to ACEA’s Vehicles on European Roads 2025 report, around 6.0 million trucks over / 3.5 tonnes were registered in the EU in 2023. The fleet had an average age of 14.1 years. / [acea.auto]

[acea.auto]

Tecvia Media / Decarbonisation in Fleet Operations / What is realistic? / For vehicles above 18 tonnes, the diesel share is likely to be slightly higher than in the overall truck fleet. This is because the fleet total also includes medium-duty distribution vehicles / between 3.5 and 18 tonnes. Battery-electric vehicles were introduced earlier and in larger numbers in this segment. / Powertrain Plausible order of magnitude in fleet over 18 t Assessment / Diesel approx. 97 to 98% clearly dominant powertrain / LNG approx. 0.5 to 1.0% focus on long-haul transport and tractor units / CNG probably below 0.2% mainly municipal, distribution and specialist vehicles / Battery-electric approx. 0.1 to 0.3% growing strongly, but still small in the total fleet / Fuel cell well below 0.01% predominantly pilot and small-series fleets / Hydrogen combustion statistically close to 0% so far mainly test and demonstration vehicles

Tecvia Media / Decarbonisation in Fleet Operations / What the statistik does not show / LNG and CNG / ACEA combines LNG and CNG under Natural Gas. The statistics therefore do not allow a / consistent Europe-wide split of the fleet into LNG and CNG trucks. / For heavy long-haul vehicles over 18 tonnes, LNG is likely to account for the clear majority within / these roughly 49,600 natural-gas trucks. CNG is more common in distribution, municipal and / specialist vehicles. However, a specific split would be an estimate rather than an officially / documented fleet figure.

Tecvia Media / Decarbonisation in Fleet Operations / What the statistik does not show / Fuel cell / Hydrogen fuel-cell trucks are not reported as a separate category in the report. Depending on / the national register, they may be listed under “Other”, “Hydrogen” or another alternative- / powertrain category. / The European Alternative Fuels Observatory records alternative powertrains for N2 and N3 / vehicle classes and lists hydrogen as a separate fuel category. The current data extend to the / second quarter of 2026. However, the publicly displayed overviews do not consistently / distinguish between fuel-cell and hydrogen internal-combustion powertrains. / [alternativ....europa.eu], [alternativ....europa.eu] / Robust assessment: The stock of fuel-cell trucks over 18 tonnes across Europe remains well / below the BEV fleet and is likely to represent only a very small fraction of one per mille of the / total fleet. A reliable Europe-wide unit count cannot be derived from publicly available / harmonised sources.

Tecvia Media / Decarbonisation in Fleet Operations / What the statistik does not show / Hydrogen internal-combustion engine / There is no separate European fleet category for trucks with hydrogen internal-combustion engines. / The vehicles deployed to date are largely demonstration, development or small-series vehicles. For this / reason, the fleet should not be described journalistically using a seemingly precise figure.

Tecvia Media / Decarbonisation in Fleet Operations / Conclusion / Around six million trucks over 3.5 tonnes are registered in the European Union. / In the latest fully available fleet year, 2023, 96.4% had diesel engines. / Natural-gas vehicles accounted for around 0.8%, while battery-electric trucks represented / about 0.1%. / Among heavy commercial vehicles over 18 tonnes, the diesel share is likely to be even / higher. / Fuel-cell trucks and vehicles with hydrogen combustion engines currently play only a marginal / role in the European fleet. / There is currently no harmonised European statistic that breaks down vehicles over 18 tonnes / by CNG, LNG, battery-electric, fuel-cell and hydrogen-combustion powertrains. [acea.auto]

Tecvia Media / Decarbonisation in Fleet Operations / Some Facts about (BIO) LNG / When natural gas was temporarily exempted from road tolls, many companies opted for this / alternative combustion-engine technology. However, as prices subsequently soared after the begining / of the Russion war (up to 5€ per kg) and the toll exemption was removed, numerous transport / companies abandoned the concept. / Now, providers such as Shell, Primagas, Verbio, Westfalen, and Green Planet Energy are once again / targeting the market - this time with Bio-LNG. / Manufacturers have further developed their vehicles, creating a viable business case that also / facilitates decarbonization, even without the toll exemption. / Advantages: approximately 25 percent lower carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions; when used as a bio- / fuel, it is nearly CO2-neutral (a 90% reduction) virtually no particulate emissions (soot) no need for / complex exhaust aftertreatment systems (such as SCR technology, exhaust gas recirculation, or / particulate filters).

Tecvia Media / Decarbonisation in Fleet Operations / Operation with Bio-LNG / • The current price for bio-CNG/LNG ranges between approximately €0.30 and / €0.50 per liter or kilogram. / • Based on an approximate calculation - assuming a fuel consumption ratio of / roughly 1:1 between diesel and natural gas - the fuel costs are significantly / lower than those for a diesel-powered truck. / • Repair and maintenance costs are approximately 10–15% higher than for diesel / vehicles. / • The additional cost when purchasing the vehicle (depending on the / manufacturer) is roughly €25,000 to €40,000. / • Tip: Consider a full-service lease with a vehicle return option. / • Based on experience to date, LNG is particularly worthwhile when vehicles / cover high annual mileages (exceeding 130,000 km/year) and when the / purchase price of the vehicles is not significantly higher than that of a diesel / truck.

Tecvia Media / Decarbonisation in Fleet Operations / Charging / Conclusion / In the EU, almost 1.18 million public charging points were installed in October 2026. Germany / had more than 214,000 charging points at the beginning of September, including around / 56,600 fast-charging points. The public truck-charging network is considerably smaller: across / Europe, the EU observatory recorded around 2,400 charging points suitable for heavy-duty / vehicles rated at 350 kW or more at 373 high-power sites in April 2026. In Germany, figures / vary depending on the definition, ranging from around 70 dedicated truck-charging stations to / almost 150 operational truck-charging locations. Despite the first corridors and charging / parks, genuine megawatt charging is still at an early stage of deployment. / Conclusion: For passenger cars and light commercial vehicles, the main issue is no longer / simply the number of charging points but their power, distribution and availability. For heavy- / duty trucking, however, a comprehensive high-power network suitable for articulated vehicles / is still lacking. Expansion is therefore shifting from individual CCS locations towards drive- / through charging parks with charging points rated between 400 kW and 1 MW.

sources.title: Interview "Mind the gap: logistics in 2027" (Laura Huefano Torres and Johannes Meuer, GSLS 2026)

pages.text: Mind the gap: logistics in 2027 / The first Global Sustainable Logistics Survey (GSLS) asked 1,085 professionals in 64 countries how the sector is progressing towards a climate-compatible future. The answer: logistics knows what works – the challenge is putting it into practice. Laura Huefano Torres, GSLS Lead and Professor Dr. Johannes Meuer, Associate Professor for Sustainability Strategy and Operations at Kühne Logistics University, set out five developments to watch in 2027. / Logistics underpins the world economy, yet its progress towards a climate-compatible future has never been measured at a global level. The 2026 Global Sustainable Logistics Survey (GSLS), led by Kühne Logistics University (KLU) and the Kuehne Climate Center (KCC), set out to change that. Professionals from 64 countries and 12 UN subregions rated 21 sustainability solutions, identified salient skills and assessed the climate risks the sector faces. It is the first in an annual series that will run throughout the UN Decade of Sustainable Transport (2026–2035). / The headline finding challenges a common assumption. Logistics providers and the shippers who buy their services rate the 21 solutions almost identically, and consider nearly all of them effective. The gap lies not in knowledge but in practice: too few effective solutions have moved beyond pilot projects into everyday operations. The question for the sector is no longer whether or what, but how and how fast. / Infrastructure becomes the bottleneck / The widest gaps between perceived effectiveness and adoption are in low-carbon fuels, fuelling and charging infrastructure, and fleet electrification. What separates widely adopted solutions from the rest is feasibility, not conviction. Low-carbon fuels for shipping and aviation are likely to stay below scale, with mandates and market-based measures delivering only modest growth. / These solutions depend on parts of the system that move at different speeds. Electric trucks are getting cheaper as production grows, helped by a wave of affordable vehicles and batteries. Volatile fuel prices as well as energy-security concerns strengthen the case for electrification. Yet, charging networks, intermodal terminals and rail capacity are not keeping pace, because they rely on planning, permits and grid connections. In 2027, grid capacity and affordable power are likely to become the bottleneck, leaving more fleets ready before the networks they need. / Given the current geo-political situation, waiting for reliable policies is a risky option. Instead, managers should invest ahead of legislation rather than wait for it. Practical starting points include electrifying frequent, regular, full-load routes that do not rely on public charging, and prioritising public infrastructure at hubs and busy corridors. Coordination will matter as much as capital. Buyers' alliances, which pool demand so that suppliers can invest, have already delivered results in individual markets and are likely to spread to new regions. With finance still risk-averse, offtake agreements, guarantees and other ways of de-risking investment upfront are likely to become a condition for scaling, not an option. In emerging markets, blended finance built on bankable offtake will need to grow across every mode. / Carbon pricing goes in-house / Carbon pricing is one of the survey's biggest surprises. It is rated effective and needs neither public authority nor infrastructure – any company can adopt its own internal carbon price – yet it remains among the least adopted solutions. / The case for it is growing stronger. From 2028, the EU's second Emissions Trading System will put a price on road transport fuels, and fuel-price shocks have exposed the sector's dependence on fossil fuels, boosting demand for electrification and alternative fuels. Companies without a medium-term transition plan for their fleets risk owning vehicles that lose value before the end of their useful life. An internal carbon price lets them test investment decisions against that future cost now, before an external price applies. Market-based measures more widely are likely to gain acceptance as registries strengthen and AI-enabled verification makes claims easier to trust. / Skills, not technology, set the pace / Education and training is rated the most feasible of all 21 solutions, yet adoption lags behind. As a relatively inexpensive measure that strengthens every other solution, it is among the easiest barriers to remove – and as AI starts to redesign logistics operations, from route and charge planning to autonomous vehicles, digital skills will only grow in value. / Three technical skills stand out as both critical and scarce: emissions calculation and reporting, knowledge of sustainable transport technology, and digital sustainability tools. Shortages are most acute in Latin America, Sub-Saharan Africa and parts of Asia. / Europe shows a different pattern. In Western Europe, 43% of respondents report a shortage of systems thinking, compared with around 19% elsewhere, while 35–38% in Northern and Western Europe report a lack of boardroom engagement. Emissions accounting is advancing globally, but regional differences persist and smaller firms are falling behind. Regions that have built measurement capability, often through mandatory reporting, now face higher-level challenges. For European operators in 2027, the priority may be less about measuring emissions and more about making sure boards act on the results. / Adaptation reaches the boardroom / The physical effects of climate change on logistics were hard to ignore in 2026. In late May, temperatures across northern India stayed above 45°C for days. In mid-July, a Canadian National freight train was trapped by wildfires in Ontario. On 14 August, the Rhine at Kaub fell below 10cm, its lowest level since records began in 1880. / The survey reveals a gap between expectation and readiness. While 83% of respondents believe adaptation will require a fundamental redesign of logistics networks, only 45% consider current efforts adequate. Geopolitics adds to the pressure, as near-shoring shifts production towards emerging industrial hubs and redraws trade lanes. In Europe that share falls to 23%, the lowest of any region. Extreme heat ranks as the most pressing climate risk in every transport mode and every region. / There is encouragement too: 77% see adaptation as aligned with decarbonisation rather than in competition with it. The three measures rated most effective – climate-proofing infrastructure, scenario-based risk assessment and digital risk monitoring – help against every type of hazard, so investing in them builds general resilience. Climate risk also belongs in investment decisions and asset renewals. Trucks typically operate for eight to 15 years and vessels for 25 to 30, so assets commissioned now must be specified for the climate in which they will operate. / A seat at the policy table / The slow spread of effective solutions, the skills shortage and the climate vulnerability of logistics all call for structural measures and clear political direction. Logistics is usually treated as part of transport, a field dominated by passenger travel. Freight and warehousing must move in the centre of national adaptation plans in line with their economic exposure. That matters as road-freight policy converges worldwide, with ambitious targets ramping up in Asia, Latin America and Africa. The GSLS 2026 offers 22 recommendations – ten for policymakers and 12 for managers – that share a common premise: policymakers should remove the barriers only they can address, notably by speeding up permits and approvals, while managers should invest ahead of legislation rather than wait for it. / Join GSLS 2027 / The value of the survey depends on who takes part. The more professionals from every mode, region and side of the market, the sharper the picture becomes. Data collection for GSLS 2027 opens in April 2027, Focus readers are more than welcomed among the respondents. Sign up to be notified of the launch at globalsustainablelogisticssurvey.org, where the full 2026 report and a short report in six languages are also available.
